situation.summary: Move-out remedial job at 18 Brindle Row, after the former tenant left on 27 August and returned his keys. On 7 September the landlord approved "the remedial works" with no price limit, but the agency had told the contractor in writing to quote only and not start without written authority. The contractor says he misread this, completed the work on 9 September, and has no recorded access arrangement, quote, or agreed scope. His £174 invoice arrived on 11 September with no explanation or completion evidence, includes a replacement blind and carpet reinstatement beyond the listed repairs, and the landlord has not been told about the work or the invoice.
situation.task: Decide how to handle the £174 invoice for work started without a quote or written authority, including the unrecorded entry and the scope change, before anyone pays, forwards or disputes it.
situation.stageLabel: Invoice received for work done without a quote or written authority; decision needed
situation.whoseMove: Waiting on the agency's own escalation owner (a person with authority over spend, key use and any tenant recharge; not named in the records) to decide the invoice and the access question. Hold payment and do not present the invoice to the landlord as approved. Routine facts can go out meanwhile: to Rowan Pike (Alder & Finch Repairs), ask for the attendance date and time, who gave access and how, an itemised price with VAT basis, completion photos and his written explanation of the instruction he received. Ivo Marlow (landlord) should hear about the completed works, the blind replacement and the £174 from the agency, once the escalation owner has reviewed them. Tomas Venn (former tenant) has no open ask to the agency that has been answered.

decision.message:
Dear Rowan,

Re: 18 Brindle Row, Larkspur Vale, ZZ1 1ZZ – invoice NBL-019-INV-11 (£174.00)

Thank you for sending the invoice this morning. When we spoke on 10 September you said you would send it that evening with the paperwork. Only the invoice has arrived. Before we can put it to the landlord, please send the following:

1. Completion photos (or a short completion report) for each of the six items: lounge floorboard and carpet, front lounge blind, under-stairs cupboard handle, kitchen blind, bathroom toilet seat, and front-gate hinge.
2. An itemised breakdown of the £174.00, with labour and materials for each item, and whether VAT applies and is included.
3. Why the front lounge blind was replaced with a new Venetian blind rather than repaired, and why the floorboard was replaced. The inspection asked for a repair to the blind and to a cracked section of flooring.
4. The date and time you attended, and how you got into the property: who gave you access, which keys you used, and where those keys are now. The former tenant had already moved out and returned his keys, and we have no record of an access arrangement.
5. A short written note of the instruction you understood you had. Our email of 7 September asked for a quotation only and said no work should start until we had reviewed the price and given written authority.

Please reply by email by the end of Friday 12 September. Until we have these details the invoice is on hold. This is a request for information. It does not approve or accept the invoice, and it does not authorise any further work. If any of the repairs is not holding, especially the gate hinge, please tell us straight away.

Kind regards,
Maya Chen
Property Manager, Northbridge Lettings
decision.rationale: The work is reported done (E013) and an invoice has arrived (E014, E016, A1). But it came without the paperwork the contractor promised on 10 September (E013), and there is no completion evidence (E015). The invoice is a single sum with no itemised prices or VAT basis (A1). It also bills more than the inspection asked for: the blind was replaced rather than repaired, and the floorboard was replaced with the carpet reinstated (S:initial-request vs A1). The playbook says: when an invoice has no evidence, chase the contractor for it, and query differences in scope or amount with the contractor before forwarding anything to the landlord. Refinement 1 adds that access is a conflicting detail to settle with the party who knows. The tenant had left and returned his keys (E003), the agency holds a set (E007), and no access arrangement is recorded. The landlord approved remedial works with no price limit (E005), so £174 may sit within his approval. That makes this a fact-finding step for now, not escalation. If the answers show unauthorised key use or a disputed price, escalate then with the full facts. The landlord was last told that scheduling was underway (E009), which is now out of date. Under refinements 9 and 10 he gets an honest status update and a date by which he will hear more.
decision.expectedOutcome: Rowan sends photos or a completion report, an itemised price with the VAT basis, reasons for the replacements, and how he got in and where the keys are. The agency can then send the invoice to the landlord with evidence and the scope changes named, or escalate if the access or price answers are a problem.
boundaries: The contractor's word and an invoice are not evidence that the work was completed or done well.
This chase does not accept, approve or dispute the £174 invoice.
The landlord's general approval to proceed does not confirm he agreed to replacing the blind and floorboard rather than repairing them.
Nothing here decides whether any cost can be recharged to the former tenant.
How the contractor got into the property and where the keys are is not yet established.

If keys were used without authority or cannot be found, or the contractor's account conflicts with the record, escalate to a person about key control.
Any recharge to the former tenant needs a person to decide it against the check-in and check-out records.
Note that the tenant's number was sent to the contractor unnecessarily (E010), and act on the tenant's request to update the records (E003).
Close only after the landlord has been told and the invoice is settled, and the keys are confirmed back at the office.

The agency's key set is the only likely way in, but this has not been confirmed.

decision.message:
ESCALATION – 18 Brindle Row, Larkspur Vale – move-out remedial works – Alder & Finch Repairs invoice NBL-019-INV-11, £174.00

Decision needed: (1) whether to accept, query or dispute the invoice, given the work was done without the quote or written authority we asked for; (2) a review of how the contractor got into the vacant property; (3) how and when to present the work and invoice to the landlord, including the items where the scope grew.

Facts on record:
- 4 Sep: move-out inspection listed six items: cracked chipboard flooring by the fireplace; a living-room front-window blind needing repair; a loose under-stairs cupboard handle; a kitchen blind not working properly; a loose toilet seat; and a front-gate bottom hinge detached from the brick pillar. No photos on file.
- 4 Sep: the former tenant, Tomas Venn, said he vacated and returned his keys on 27 Aug and could not give access. He asked for the records to be updated. No action on that request is recorded.
- 7 Sep: the landlord, Ivo Marlow, replied: "Yes, I am happy for you to proceed with the remedial works." He gave no price limit or conditions, and no estimate had been sent to him.
- 7 Sep: we asked Alder & Finch (Rowan Pike) in writing for a quotation only. The email said no work was to be done until we had reviewed the price and issued written authority. It also asked for inspection windows and access requirements. The agency holds a key set.
- 7 Sep: the landlord was told that scheduling was underway with the tenant and the provider. He has had no update since.
- 8 Sep: our chase to the contractor included the former tenant's phone number, although he had said he had left. This may need a privacy review.
- 10 Sep (call): Rowan said he thought he had been told to do the work, and that he completed it on 9 Sep. We do not know how he got access, who released keys, or whether the keys came back.
- 11 Sep: invoice of £174.00 received. It is a single lump sum with no itemised prices and no VAT basis. It has no covering message, photos or completion report. It bills a replacement floorboard with the carpet reinstated, and a new Venetian blind supplied and fitted in place of the lounge blind. The inspection had asked for a blind repair and did not mention carpet. No written authority or approved variation is on record.
- The 10 Sep note saying to wait for an invoice is out of date. The invoice has now arrived.

Done by me in this turn: emailed Rowan Pike asking for the visit date and time, how he got access and where the keys are now, an itemised price with VAT basis, completion photos of each item, and his written account of the instruction he worked to. Reply requested by end of Fri 12 Sep.

Recommendation: hold payment. Do not forward the invoice to the landlord as approved. Check the key log today. Once the itemised breakdown and photos arrive, send the landlord a factual update with the invoice and ask whether he accepts the blind replacement and carpet reinstatement. Do not raise any recharge to the former tenant unless the check-in and check-out records support it.
decision.rationale: There is no doubt about who owes the next move. The contractor did the work against our written "quote only, no work without written authority" instruction (E008, E013). He entered a vacant property with no access arrangement recorded, while the agency held the keys (E003, E007, E015). His £174 lump-sum invoice has no itemisation, no VAT basis and no completion evidence, and it includes scope beyond the inspection list: a new Venetian blind and carpet reinstatement (S:initial-request, E016, A1). Key control, unauthorised entry, a breached instruction and changed scope are all escalation triggers, and the decision to accept or dispute the invoice needs authority I don't have. The landlord's broad approval (E005) might cover the cost, but he never saw a price or the scope changes. The routine evidence request goes to the contractor now in alsoSend, so the person who picks this up has it to hand.
decision.expectedOutcome: The escalation owner holds payment, checks the key log and decides how to handle the invoice. The contractor sends an itemised breakdown, photos and an account of access by 12 Sep, so the landlord can then be told accurately.
boundaries: The invoice does not prove the work was done or done to standard; there are no photos or completion report.
The landlord's general approval of "remedial works" was not approval of a £174 price or of replacing the blind and reinstating carpet.
This escalation does not accept, pay or dispute the invoice.
Nothing here establishes that the former tenant is liable for any item or should be recharged.
How the contractor got access is not established.
remainingWork: Get the contractor's itemised breakdown, VAT basis, photos and account of access.
Check the agency key log and confirm the keys are back.
Update the landlord with the evidence and invoice, and get his decision on the blind replacement and carpet.
Decide invoice payment and the route for paying it.
Act on the former tenant's request to update the records (E003), and review the disclosure of his phone number (E010).
Close only once the evidence is in, the landlord has been told and the invoice is settled.
assumptions: Maya Chen cannot approve spend or decide key-control matters herself.
The completion date of 9 Sep comes only from the contractor's call (E013).
No VAT basis can be inferred from the £174.00 lump sum.

alternatives.action: landlord.update forwarding the invoice as completed works
alternatives.whyNot: There is no completion evidence, the scope changed without approval, and the work breached our instruction. Forwarding it would present unapproved spend as agreed.
This gets the evidence but leaves the key-control breach and the invoice decision without an owner. Those need a person, so the chase goes in alsoSend.
The invoice is here and the earlier instruction to wait is out of date. Nothing has been promised that we are waiting for.

What happened:

Nothing shows that was done.
- 7 Sep: the landlord, Ivo Marlow, replied: "Yes, I am happy for you to proceed with the remedial works." He gave no price limit and no conditions. The agency holds a set of keys.
- 7 Sep: we emailed Rowan Pike at Alder & Finch asking for a QUOTE ONLY, with this instruction: "do not carry out any work until Northbridge Lettings reviewed the price and issued written authority". We also asked for inspection windows and access requirements. On 8 Sep we chased him, and that chase included the former tenant's phone number.
- 10 Sep, by phone: Rowan said he thought the instruction was to do the work and that he had finished it on 9 Sep. He said he would send the invoice and paperwork that evening.

Decisions that need a person:
1. Key control and access. No access arrangement is recorded for 9 Sep. Who let the contractor in, with which keys, and have the keys come back? Entering a vacant property without authority needs a review.
2. The invoice. The contractor ignored a written quote-only instruction and replaced items instead of repairing them, with no approval. Do we accept the invoice, ask for an itemised revision, or dispute it? I have not forwarded it to the landlord or treated it as approved.
3. The landlord. He was last told on 7 Sep that "scheduling was underway". He has not heard that the work is done, that the scope changed or that an invoice has arrived. Please decide how and when he is told, and whether the replacement items go to him as a scope and price question.

final.message:
ESCALATION – 18 Brindle Row, Larkspur Vale – move-out remedial works – Alder & Finch Repairs invoice NBL-019-INV-11, £174.00

Decision needed: (1) whether to accept, query or dispute the invoice, given the work was done without the quote or written authority we asked for; (2) a review of how the contractor got into the vacant property; (3) how and when to present the work and invoice to the landlord, including the items where the scope grew.

Facts on record:
- 4 Sep: move-out inspection listed six items: cracked chipboard flooring by the fireplace; a living-room front-window blind needing repair; a loose under-stairs cupboard handle; a kitchen blind not working properly; a loose toilet seat; and a front-gate bottom hinge detached from the brick pillar. No photos on file.
- 4 Sep: the former tenant, Tomas Venn, said he vacated and returned his keys on 27 Aug and could not give access. He asked for the records to be updated. No action on that request is recorded.
- 7 Sep: the landlord, Ivo Marlow, replied: "Yes, I am happy for you to proceed with the remedial works." He gave no price limit or conditions, and no estimate had been sent to him.
- 7 Sep: we asked Alder & Finch (Rowan Pike) in writing for a quotation only. The email said no work was to be done until we had reviewed the price and issued written authority. It also asked for inspection windows and access requirements. The agency holds a key set.
- 7 Sep: the landlord was told that scheduling was underway with the tenant and the provider. He has had no update since.
- 8 Sep: our chase to the contractor included the former tenant's phone number, although he had said he had left. This may need a privacy review.
- 10 Sep (call): Rowan said he thought he had been told to do the work, and that he completed it on 9 Sep. We do not know how he got access, who released keys, or whether the keys came back.
- 11 Sep: invoice of £174.00 received. It is a single lump sum with no itemised prices and no VAT basis. It has no covering message, photos or completion report. It bills a replacement floorboard with the carpet reinstated, and a new Venetian blind supplied and fitted in place of the lounge blind. The inspection had asked for a blind repair and did not mention carpet. No written authority or approved variation is on record.
- The 10 Sep note saying to wait for an invoice is out of date. The invoice has now arrived.

Done by me in this turn: emailed Rowan Pike asking for the visit date and time, how he got access and where the keys are now, an itemised price with VAT basis, completion photos of each item, and his written account of the instruction he worked to. Reply requested by end of Fri 12 Sep.

Recommendation: hold payment. Do not forward the invoice to the landlord as approved. Check the key log today. Once the itemised breakdown and photos arrive, send the landlord a factual update with the invoice and ask whether he accepts the blind replacement and carpet reinstatement. Do not raise any recharge to the former tenant unless the check-in and check-out records support it.
final.rationale: There is no doubt about who owes the next move. The contractor did the work against our written "quote only, no work without written authority" instruction (E008, E013). He entered a vacant property with no access arrangement recorded, while the agency held the keys (E003, E007, E015). His £174 lump-sum invoice has no itemisation, no VAT basis and no completion evidence, and it includes scope beyond the inspection list: a new Venetian blind and carpet reinstatement (S:initial-request, E016, A1). Key control, unauthorised entry, a breached instruction and changed scope are all escalation triggers, and the decision to accept or dispute the invoice needs authority I don't have. The landlord's broad approval (E005) might cover the cost, but he never saw a price or the scope changes. The routine evidence request goes to the contractor now in alsoSend, so the person who picks this up has it to hand.
final.expectedOutcome: The escalation owner holds payment, checks the key log and decides how to handle the invoice. The contractor sends an itemised breakdown, photos and an account of access by 12 Sep, so the landlord can then be told accurately.
boundaries: The invoice does not prove the work was done or done to standard; there are no photos or completion report.
The landlord's general approval of "remedial works" was not approval of a £174 price or of replacing the blind and reinstating carpet.
This escalation does not accept, pay or dispute the invoice.
Nothing here establishes that the former tenant is liable for any item or should be recharged.
How the contractor got access is not established.
remainingWork: Get the contractor's itemised breakdown, VAT basis, photos and account of access.
Check the agency key log and confirm the keys are back.
Update the landlord with the evidence and invoice, and get his decision on the blind replacement and carpet.
Decide invoice payment and the route for paying it.
Act on the former tenant's request to update the records (E003), and review the disclosure of his phone number (E010).
Close only once the evidence is in, the landlord has been told and the invoice is settled.
assumptions: Maya Chen cannot approve spend or decide key-control matters herself.
The completion date of 9 Sep comes only from the contractor's call (E013).
No VAT basis can be inferred from the £174.00 lump sum.

alternatives.action: landlord.update forwarding the invoice as completed works
alternatives.whyNot: There is no completion evidence, the scope changed without approval, and the work breached our instruction. Forwarding it would present unapproved spend as agreed.
This gets the evidence but leaves the key-control breach and the invoice decision without an owner. Those need a person, so the chase goes in alsoSend.
The invoice is here and the earlier instruction to wait is out of date. Nothing has been promised that we are waiting for.

handover.summary: Alder & Finch Repairs completed six move-out items at the vacant 18 Brindle Row on 9 Sep (by their own account). Our written instruction had been to quote only and wait for written authority. Their £174.00 lump-sum invoice has no itemisation, VAT basis or photos, and covers more than the inspection asked for: a new Venetian blind, plus carpet reinstatement with the floorboard. No access arrangement is recorded, and the agency held the keys. The landlord approved "remedial works" in general but has not seen a price and has not been told the work is done.
